common-ancestry-s1.title: Human genes in yeast cells
common-ancestry-s1.html:
Baker's yeast cannot divide if it lacks any one of the six genes below. Researchers deleted one gene at a time and gave each deletion strain the matching human gene. As controls, some deletion strains received no gene and some received the yeast's own gene back. Every strain grew for 48 h at 30 °C. Growth is given as a percent of unaltered yeast (mean of 4 cultures).

continuing-evolution-s1.title: Mosquitoes after insecticide-treated bed nets
continuing-evolution-s1.html:
In year 0, bed nets treated with a pyrethroid insecticide were handed out across a farming district. Each year researchers raised mosquitoes from larvae collected in the district. They exposed 200 adult females to a standard pyrethroid dose for 1 hour and recorded the percent alive 24 hours later (mean ± 2 SE of 8 tubes). They also tested 200 mosquitoes for the kdr allele, a version of a nerve sodium-channel gene that pyrethroids bind poorly, and report its frequency among all alleles of that gene.

continuing-evolution-s2.title: Twelve bacterial populations followed for 40,000 generations
continuing-evolution-s2.html:
From a single ancestral E. coli cell, researchers started 12 populations in flasks of medium with a small amount of glucose at 37 °C. Each day they moved 1% of every culture into fresh medium, about 6.6 generations a day. Every 500 generations they froze a sample of each population; frozen cells can be revived later. To measure fitness, revived cells from one time point were grown in the same flask as revived ancestral cells (marked so the two can be told apart). Relative fitness is the evolved cells' growth divided by the ancestor's growth in that flask; 1.00 means no difference.

continuing-evolution-s3.title: A rabbit-killing virus and wild rabbits, 1951-1963
continuing-evolution-s3.html:
A virus that kills European rabbits was released in Australia in 1950 to reduce the number of wild rabbits there. Mosquitoes spread the virus by biting infected rabbits and then healthy ones. In each listed year, researchers (1) collected virus samples from wild rabbits and measured how lethal each was in lab rabbits never before exposed, and (2) caught young wild rabbits and infected them with one standard virus strain kept frozen and unchanged since the 1950s. The values are simplified for teaching, following the pattern of the field surveys.

continuing-evolution-s4.title: A model of resistance in HIV
continuing-evolution-s4.html:
The model uses rounded numbers. In a person with untreated HIV, about 1010 new virus particles are made each day. Reverse transcriptase does not proofread, so copying errors are common. For each of three drugs (A, B and C), about 1 in every 105 new viral genomes carries a mutation that lets the virus resist that drug. The three kinds of mutation arise independently of each other.

Model values
QuantityValue

Share of new genomes resistant to drug A1 in 105
Share resistant to drug B1 in 105
Share resistant to drug C1 in 105

speciation-s1.html:
Three populations of a small fish were sampled. Populations L and M share the same streams in one valley; population K lives in a separate river system 300 km away. In the lab, researchers placed 100 pairs (one female, one male) for each cross in tanks and recorded whether they spawned, how many eggs were fertilized and hatched, and whether the offspring grown to adulthood were fertile.

speciation-s2.title: A tetraploid wildflower
speciation-s2.html:
A wildflower species is diploid, with 2n = 14. In one plant, a failure of meiosis produced gametes with 14 chromosomes, and self-fertilization of that plant produced tetraploid offspring (4n = 28). The tetraploids grow among the diploids in the same meadow, flower at the same time and are visited by the same bees. Researchers then made the crosses below.

population-variation-s1.html:
In a year when rice blast fungus spread through a farming region, researchers compared three kinds of fields. Some fields grew only variety H, a high-value variety the local strain of the fungus can infect. Some grew only variety R, which carries an allele that resists the local strain. population-variation-s2.html:
Roads, farms and towns cut a population of wild cats off from all others. By the early 1990s about 26 adults remained. In 1995, eight females from a larger population of the same species in another region were released into the area, and many bred there. Researchers tested cats for genetic variation and examined kittens for inherited defects.

origin-of-life-s1.title: Amino acids in a spark experiment
origin-of-life-s1.html:
Students sealed water, methane (CH4), ammonia (NH3) and hydrogen gas (H2) in sterilized glass flasks. The water was gently boiled so vapor circulated past two electrodes. In three flasks, sparks passed between the electrodes continuously; in three control flasks, the electrodes were present but no sparks were made. Each day a small sample was tested for amino acids. Values are means of three flasks.

origin-of-life-s2.title: Clay, membranes and RNA
origin-of-life-s2.html:
In water at the right pH, fatty acids slowly assemble into vesicles: hollow spheres bounded by a membrane. Researchers mixed fatty acids with buffer under four conditions and timed how long it took for half of the fatty acid to form vesicles. In two conditions they added short RNA strands tagged with a fluorescent dye, in one case first letting the RNA stick to particles of a clay mineral. They then counted the vesicles with fluorescent RNA inside.

items.q: Which comparison in the table best shows that the percent of identical amino acids does not by itself predict whether a human gene can replace the yeast gene?
options: The nucleotide enzyme (46%, grows) and the replication-complex protein (58%, no growth)
The glycolysis enzyme (53%, grows) and the ribosomal protein (61%, grows)
The replication-complex protein (58%, no growth) and the mitosis protein (31%, no growth)
The sterol enzyme (49%, grows) and the glycolysis enzyme (53%, grows)

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the human glycolysis gene restoring growth to yeast that lack their own version?
options: Yeast and humans inherited this enzyme and the genetic code from a shared ancestor, so yeast can build a working enzyme from it
The human gene mutated inside the yeast cells until its sequence matched the missing yeast gene, so the yeast enzyme was made again
The two enzymes have the same amino acid sequence, so the yeast cell makes exactly its own enzyme from the human gene
Glycolysis arose separately in the ancestors of yeast and of humans, and the two versions happen to catalyze the same steps

items.q: What is the control in which the yeast's own gene is put back mainly designed to rule out?
options: That the gene-transfer method itself harms growth, which would make failures with human genes meaningless
That the yeast cells could grow well without the deleted gene, so the gene was not essential for division
That the human genes were too long for the yeast's ribosomes to translate into complete proteins
That the growth medium lacked a nutrient yeast needs, so no strain could grow well at 30 °C

items.q: When lined up, the yeast and human ribosomal proteins can be compared at 200 positions. Using the table, how many of those 200 positions carry different amino acids? Give a whole number.
A student concludes from these results that humans evolved from yeast. Which response is best supported by the data and by evolutionary theory?
options: The data fit humans and yeast descending from a shared ancestor; modern yeast is a distant relative, not an ancestor
The data support the conclusion, since four human genes can do the job of yeast genes and so came from yeast originally
The data contradict any relationship, because two of the six human genes failed to work in yeast
The data show that humans and yeast are close relatives, since their proteins are identical at about half of their positions

items.q: Which pairing of organism and domain is supported by the table?
options: X: Archaea
Z: Archaea
W: Eukarya
Y: Bacteria

items.q: Select the two features in the table that are evidence that W, X, Y and Z share one common ancestor.
options: Reading mRNA with the standard genetic code
Making ATP with an ATP synthase in a membrane
DNA wrapped around histone proteins
Ether links in membrane lipids
A circular main chromosome

items.q: Which evidence from the table best supports the claim that X shares a more recent common ancestor with Y than with W?
options: X and Y both wrap their DNA around histones, and W does not
X and W both lack a nucleus, and Y has one
X and Y both lack peptidoglycan in a cell wall, and W has it
X and W both have a circular main chromosome, and Y does not

items.q: Penicillin stops cells from building peptidoglycan. If each organism is grown with penicillin, whose growth is expected to be slowed?
options: W and Z
W, but not X, Y or Z
X and Y
W, X and Z, the three prokaryotes

items.q: Which step in making a protein takes place in Y's cells but not in W's?
options: Introns are spliced out of the RNA transcript in the nucleus
Ribosomes translate the mRNA's codons into a chain of amino acids
RNA polymerase transcribes a gene into RNA
A start codon sets the reading frame of the mRNA

items.q: Which feature is found in every eukaryote but in no prokaryote?
options: A nucleus
Ribosomes
A plasma membrane
DNA as genetic material

items.q: Which reasoning best explains why a nearly universal genetic code is strong evidence that all life shares one ancestor?
options: Many different codes would work equally well, so separate origins of life would be unlikely to arrive at the same one
The chemistry of the four bases fixes which amino acid each codon stands for, so any life anywhere would use this code
Organisms frequently trade codon tables with neighbors by gene transfer, so the code spread across life
The code changes quickly, so organisms with the same code probably shared an ancestor recently

items.q: In human mitochondria the codon UGA codes for tryptophan instead of stop, and some single-celled ciliates read UAA as glutamine. How do these facts affect the claim that all life shares one ancestor?
options: They fit the claim: a few small changes in a code that is otherwise the same are expected after shared descent
They weaken the claim: mitochondria and ciliates probably arose separately from other life, each with a code of its own
They disprove the claim, since one exception shows that the genetic code is not shared
They are unrelated to the claim, because the genetic code says nothing about ancestry

items.q: Which observation supports the idea that Archaea share a more recent common ancestor with eukaryotes than with Bacteria?
options: Archaeal RNA polymerase and histones are built like those of eukaryotes
Archaea and Bacteria both lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
Many archaea live in hot springs and salt flats where few eukaryotes live
Archaeal ribosomes are about the same size as bacterial ribosomes

items.q: The protein histone H4 in peas and in cows differs at only 2 of its 102 amino acids. Which explanation best accounts for so few differences?
options: Most changes to H4 disrupt DNA packing, so carriers left fewer offspring and the changes were lost
The gene for H4 is protected from mutation, so its DNA sequence has not been copied with errors
Peas and cows share a fairly recent common ancestor, so there has been too little time for many changes
H4 is made of nucleic acid, so its sequence is copied more accurately than a protein's

items.q: Researchers compare two genes between mice and humans. Gene F codes for a core ribosome protein, where most amino acid changes stop the ribosome from working. Gene P codes for a protein whose exact sequence matters little. Predict the value for gene F compared with gene P.

variables.name: Number of amino acid differences between the mouse and human proteins
Rate at which new mutations arise in the gene's DNA
Share of amino acid-changing mutations that persist over many generations
Number of silent base differences that leave the amino acid unchanged

items.q: Which statement describes the last universal common ancestor (LUCA)?
options: The most recent population of cells from which every living organism descends
The very first living cell to appear on Earth, before any other kind of life existed
A single bacterium alive today that is the parent of the other species on Earth
An early eukaryote whose nucleus was passed to Bacteria and Archaea

items.q: Bacteria and Archaea build their membranes from different kinds of lipids. A student argues that the two groups therefore cannot share a common ancestor. Which response best counters the argument?
options: Both share a lipid bilayer, the genetic code, ribosomes and ATP; one feature can change after two lines split
Both groups lack a nucleus, so they belong to one group, and their lipids turn out to be the same on closer study
Lipids are not coded directly by genes, so differences in lipids say nothing useful about ancestry
Archaea took their lipids from eukaryotes, which explains why they differ from bacterial lipids

items.q: Some antibiotics that bind bacterial ribosomes can also slow protein synthesis inside human mitochondria, causing side effects. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: Mitochondria descend from bacteria, and their ribosomes still resemble bacterial ribosomes
Mitochondria make most of the cell's proteins, so drugs that affect ribosomes act on them first
The antibiotics are converted into human hormones that enter the mitochondria
Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are identical to bacterial ribosomes, and mitochondria take them up

items.q: A new single-celled eukaryote is discovered in a lake. Select the two features you can predict it has, based on the features eukaryotes share.
options: Genes with introns that are spliced out of RNA
Membrane-bound organelles
A cell wall containing peptidoglycan
Ether links in its membrane lipids
A single circular chromosome with no histones

items.q: Between which two consecutive years did the frequency of the kdr allele rise the most?
options: Year 3 to year 4
Year 4 to year 5
Year 5 to year 6
Year 7 to year 8

items.q: Calculate the mean rate of increase in kdr allele frequency from year 2 to year 6, in percentage points per year. Give one decimal place.
The kdr allele already had a frequency of 5% in year 0, before any nets were used. Which explanation best fits the data and how evolution works?
options: The allele arose by random mutation before the nets, and the insecticide then favored mosquitoes already carrying it
Mosquitoes that touched the nets formed the kdr mutation in response, and then passed it to their offspring
The nets made each mosquito's sodium channels change shape gradually during its life, and the change was inherited
The kdr allele was carried into the district by the nets themselves, which were made in a place with resistant mosquitoes

items.q: In year 8 the nets are replaced with nets treated with an insecticide that acts on a different target. Mosquitoes carrying kdr survive slightly less well than others when no pyrethroid is present. Predict the kdr frequency over the next several years.
options: It falls slowly, because carriers now have slightly lower fitness than other mosquitoes
It stays at 72%, because the allele no longer affects survival once pyrethroids are gone
It drops to zero within a year, because mosquitoes stop making the resistant channel when it is not needed
It keeps rising toward 100%, because the new insecticide also kills the mosquitoes that lack kdr

items.q: A student claims the nets caused the rise in kdr. Which additional data would most strengthen the claim?
options: kdr frequencies over the same years in a similar nearby district where no treated nets were used
kdr frequencies measured twice as often, at 6-month intervals, in the same district with the treated nets
The number of mosquitoes caught each year in the district with treated nets, before and after year 0
Survival of the same mosquitoes after a dose of the pyrethroid twice as strong as the standard dose

items.q: Calculate the mean gain in relative fitness per 1,000 generations between generation 0 and generation 2,000. Give two decimal places.
Which statement best describes the change in mean relative fitness?
options: It rose quickly at first, then kept rising more slowly through generation 40,000
It rose at a steady rate, gaining the same amount in each block of 1,000 generations
It rose until generation 10,000 and stayed exactly the same after that
It rose slowly at first and then faster and faster as mutations piled up

items.q: Why does freezing samples every 500 generations make the fitness measurements more reliable?
options: Ancestral and evolved cells can be revived and grown together in one flask under the same conditions
Freezing stops new mutations, so the evolved populations have the same genes as the ancestor when tested
Freezing kills the least fit cells, so the cells measured are mostly the ones with beneficial mutations
Frozen samples let researchers skip the daily transfers and still reach 40,000 generations sooner

items.q: Using the ± 2 SE intervals, which conclusion is supported?
options: Fitness at 40,000 generations differs from fitness at 5,000, but 10,000 and 20,000 are not shown to differ
Each mean in the table differs from the mean before it, because each one is higher than the last
The means at generations 20,000 and 40,000 differ from each other, because their two intervals do not overlap
The means are not shown to differ, because each interval overlaps with the one after it

items.q: All 12 populations gained fitness, though each gained it through mostly different mutations. What does this best suggest?
options: The shared conditions selected for faster growth, while which mutations arose differed by chance
The ancestor already carried the beneficial mutations, so the 12 flasks needed no new mutations
Genetic drift by itself raised fitness, since drift tends to move separate populations in one direction
The populations exchanged genes during the daily transfers, so the 12 ended with matching mutations

items.q: Which statement best describes how the virus samples changed from 1951 to 1963?
options: The most lethal type became rare, and samples killing 70-99% became the most common type
The least lethal samples became the most common type, so the virus stopped killing rabbits
The virus samples stayed equally lethal, and the changes came from the rabbits alone
The most lethal type became more common each year as the virus adapted to rabbits

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the change in the virus?
options: Rabbits with less lethal virus stayed alive and infectious longer, so mosquitoes spread that virus more
The virus evolved to be less lethal so that it would not wipe out the rabbits it depends on
Less lethal viruses copied themselves faster inside each rabbit, so they outgrew the most lethal type
Lab rabbits became more resistant over the years, so the same viruses appeared less lethal in tests

items.q: Which data are the best evidence that the wild rabbits themselves evolved?
options: Deaths from the unchanged standard strain fell from 90% to 30% of wild rabbits
The share of virus samples killing over 99% of lab rabbits fell from 100% to 1%
The share of virus samples killing under 70% of lab rabbits rose from 0% to 31%
The share of samples killing 70-99% of lab rabbits rose from 0% to about 70%

items.q: Wild rabbits caught in 1963 are infected with a virus sample frozen in 1951, of the type that killed over 99% of lab rabbits. Predict the outcome.
options: Fewer die than among 1951 rabbits given the same virus, but the share killed is still high
The same share die as in 1951, because the 1951 virus is unchanged by freezing
Almost no 1963 rabbits die, because they are now resistant to the virus in its many forms
More of the 1963 rabbits die than in 1951, because the rabbits have not met this virus type in years

items.q: A patient takes drug A alone. According to the model, how many new virus particles resistant to drug A are made per day before the drug starts to act? Give a whole number.
According to the model, how many new particles per day are expected to resist both drug A and drug B at once? Give a whole number.
Why do doctors give all three drugs at the same time rather than one drug and then another when the first stops working?
options: One at a time, virus resistant to the first drug multiplies until a mutant resistant to the next appears
Giving the drugs one after another wears the patient's immune system down faster than giving them together
Each drug works well just when the other two are present, because they bind one enzyme together
Giving one drug at a time causes the virus to make new resistance mutations in response to each drug in turn

items.q: A patient on all three drugs often skips doses, so the drugs fall to low levels for days at a time and the virus multiplies again. Predict the effect on each quantity.

variables.name: Number of new virus particles made per day
Chance that a particle resistant to all three drugs arises over the next year
Share of new genomes carrying a given resistance mutation, before any selection

items.q: A new flu vaccine is made every year. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: Mutations change its surface proteins, and immunity in people favors variants that antibodies bind poorly
The flu virus has a fixed set of strains, and the vaccine rotates through them in a yearly cycle
Antibodies made in response to a vaccine break down within a few weeks, so a new formula is needed
Each year's vaccine causes new mutations in the virus, so next year's vaccine is changed to match them

items.q: Glyphosate kills plants by blocking the enzyme EPSPS. Weeds that survive glyphosate on many farms carry 40 to 100 copies of the EPSPS gene, while susceptible weeds of the same kind carry one. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Extra copies arose by duplication and make so much enzyme that some escapes the herbicide; spraying favored them
Glyphosate entered the weeds' cells and copied the EPSPS gene, raising its copy number in each sprayed plant
Each extra copy carries a mutation that changes the enzyme's shape so that glyphosate no longer binds to its active site
The surviving weeds absorbed less glyphosate, and their extra gene copies have no effect on their survival

items.q: Select the two observations that show evolution happening in a population today.
options: The frequency of an allele in a wild population is measured each year and rises over 15 years
Bacterial samples frozen in 1990 and in 2020 from one population differ by dozens of new mutations
A single insect sprayed many times during its life becomes harder to kill
A fossil shell from deep rock layers looks different from shells of the same kind alive today
A wild population's average beak size stays the same while its habitat is unchanged

items.q: On the Hawaiian island of Kauai, flies that lay their eggs in crickets find male crickets by their song. Within about 20 generations, most males there carried a mutation that leaves their wings unable to make sound. Which explanation fits these observations best?
options: Silent males were found by flies less often, so they lived to mate more and the mutation spread
Males stopped singing because they learned the song attracted flies, and this learning was inherited
The flies caused the wing mutation in the males they attacked, so it spread through the population
Silent males attracted more females, so the mutation spread even though flies ignored the song

items.q: Where rough-skinned newts carry high levels of a nerve toxin, the garter snakes that eat them have sodium channels the toxin binds poorly; where newts carry little toxin, snakes are easily paralyzed by it. Which term and explanation fit best?
options: Coevolution: each species is a selective pressure on the other, so toxin and resistance escalate
Artificial selection: people living near the newts have bred snakes that are resistant to the toxin
Convergent evolution: newts and snakes evolved the same toxin separately because they share a habitat
Genetic drift: resistance became common by chance in places where newts happen to be toxic

items.q: In one of 12 lab populations of E. coli, cells able to grow on citrate appeared after about 31,000 generations. When researchers revived frozen samples from that population and let them evolve again, citrate use reappeared in some replays started from samples after generation 20,000, and in none started from earlier samples. What does this most suggest?
options: A mutation arising before generation 20,000 was needed before a later mutation could produce citrate use
Citrate use required 31,000 generations of steady exposure to citrate, so the earlier samples had too little time to evolve it
The revived samples from before generation 20,000 had lost the ability to mutate after being frozen
Citrate use was present in the ancestor and was switched on by the environment after generation 20,000

items.q: Which organism should be used as the outgroup, and why?
options: The green alga, because other evidence places it outside the land-plant group
The oak, because it has the most characters and so has changed the most from the ancestor
The moss, because among the land plants it has the fewest of the characters scored
The fern, because it falls in the middle of the table and can be compared with both ends

items.q: Which cladogram is best supported by the table?
options: Pine and oak are sister taxa, the fern joins them next, and the moss joins that group next
Moss and fern are sister taxa, and pine and oak are sister taxa, joined to them at one node
Fern and pine are sister taxa, oak joins them next, and the moss joins that group next
Oak branches off first among the land plants, then the pine, the fern and finally the moss

items.q: A classmate proposes a tree in which the fern branches off first among the land plants, then the moss, with pine and oak as sister taxa. Counting each gain or loss of a character as one change, what is the smallest number of changes this tree needs to account for the four characters? Give a whole number.
Which character is a shared derived character that groups the pine with the oak but not with the fern?
options: Seeds
Vascular tissue
Embryo develops inside the parent plant
Flowers

items.q: On the cladogram best supported by the table, select the two groups that are clades.
options: Fern, pine and oak
Pine and oak
Moss and fern
Green alga and moss
Moss, pine and oak

items.q: Which node represents the most recent common ancestor of the mouse and the turtle?
options: Node 1
Node 2
Node 3
Node 5

items.q: Which statement is supported by the tree?
options: The turtle is equally related to the crocodile and to the sparrow
The crocodile is more closely related to the lizard than to the sparrow
The lizard is more closely related to the turtle than the sparrow is
The frog is the ancestor from which the other six animals evolved

items.q: Select the two groups that are clades on this tree.
options: Crocodile and sparrow
Turtle, crocodile and sparrow
Lizard, snake, turtle and crocodile
Mouse, lizard and snake
Frog and mouse

items.q: A newly described fossil animal has a bony skull feature found in crocodiles and birds but not in turtles, lizards or snakes. Where on the tree does the fossil most likely belong?
options: On the line between node 5 and node 6, or within the crocodile-sparrow group
On a branch joining the line between node 3 and node 4, near the lizard and snake
On a branch joining the turtle's line, because the turtle is closest to the crocodile
Below node 1, because a fossil is older than the living animals on the tree

items.q: A student says lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles form a natural group, separate from birds, because they all have scales and do not keep a constant body temperature. Which response is best supported by the tree?
options: It leaves out the sparrow, which also descends from node 3, so it is not a clade
The group is a clade, because scales are a shared derived character that birds have lost
The group is a clade, because node 3 is the common ancestor of these four animals
The group would be a clade if the mouse were added, because the mouse is also outside the birds

items.q: Which tree is best supported by the DNA differences?
options: Human and chimpanzee are sister taxa; the gorilla joins them next, then the orangutan, with the macaque branching off first
Chimpanzee and gorilla are sister taxa; the human joins them next, then the orangutan, with the macaque branching off first
Human branches off first, then the macaque; chimpanzee, gorilla and orangutan form a group of three
Orangutan and gorilla are sister taxa; human and chimpanzee join them, with the macaque branching off first

items.q: Assume differences build up at a constant rate. Using the orangutan split as a calibration, estimate how many million years ago the human and chimpanzee lines split. Give one decimal place.
Using the same molecular clock, about when did the macaque line split from the line leading to the apes?
options: About 30 million years ago
About 62 million years ago
About 15 million years ago
About 7.5 million years ago

items.q: Which assumption must hold for these time estimates to be reliable?
options: Differences in this DNA region build up at about the same rate in each of these primate lines
This DNA region codes for an important protein, so changes in it are removed by selection
The five primates have the same body size and live in the same kind of habitat
Each primate line has gained the same number of new characters since it split off

items.q: The researchers repeat the study with a 1,000-base stretch of a gene coding for an essential enzyme, in which most changes harm the enzyme. Predict the results.
options: Fewer differences in each pair but the same branching pattern; dating needs this gene's own calibration
The same numbers of differences, because each stretch of DNA mutates at the same rate in a given line
More differences in each pair, because essential genes are copied less accurately than the rest of the genome
A different branching pattern, with the macaque now closest to the human, because the enzyme is more important

items.q: Four-chambered hearts are found in mammals, crocodiles and birds, while lizards, snakes and turtles have three-chambered hearts. Crocodiles and birds are each other's closest living relatives, and lizards, snakes and turtles share a more recent ancestor with crocodiles and birds than any of them shares with mammals. Which explanation is most parsimonious?
options: Four chambers arose twice: once in the mammal line and once in the ancestor of crocodiles and birds
Four chambers arose once, in the ancestor of mammals and reptiles, and were lost in lizards, snakes and turtles
Four chambers arose three separate times, once each in mammals, crocodiles and birds
Four chambers arose once in mammals and were passed to crocodiles and birds by interbreeding

items.q: On a tree of mammals, humans are drawn at the top tip. A student concludes that humans are the most evolved mammal on the tree. Which response is correct?
options: All living tips have evolved for equally long since the root, and tip order can be rotated freely
The student is right, because a tree lists organisms from the least to the most evolved
The student is right if humans are also the tip farthest from the root
The order of the tips shows the order in which each organism appeared on Earth, so humans appeared last

items.q: A tree has the nested grouping ((P, (Q, R)), S), drawn with the tips in the order P, Q, R, S from top to bottom. Which statement is correct?
options: R is more closely related to P than to S
R is more closely related to S, since their tips are drawn side by side
P is equally closely related to Q and to S
S is the ancestor of P, Q and R, since it branches off first

items.q: Whales were long classified apart from hoofed mammals. DNA studies then placed whales inside the even-toed hoofed mammals, closest to hippos, and fossil early whales were later found with ankle bones of the shape found only in that group. What does this history best show?
options: A tree is a hypothesis that is revised when new molecular and fossil evidence is found
DNA data are usually wrong when they disagree with body features, so the old grouping stands
Whales evolved from hippos living today, which explains why the two are so similar
Classification depends on where an animal lives, so whales belong with other sea animals

items.q: The lion is Panthera leo, the tiger is Panthera tigris and the house cat is Felis catus. Based on their names, which pair is most closely related?
options: Lion and tiger
Lion and house cat
Tiger and house cat
The three are equally related

items.q: The forelimbs of a bat, a whale and a human contain the same set of bones, arranged and shaped differently for flying, swimming and grasping. Which process best explains this?
options: Divergent evolution: descendants of one ancestor adapted to different ways of life
Convergent evolution: unrelated animals evolved the same bones separately because they faced the same needs
Coevolution: the three species evolved their forelimbs in response to one another
Genetic drift: the three forelimbs became different by chance, with no role for selection

items.q: In a study of relationships among mammals only, why is "has a backbone" of no help in grouping the mammals?
options: All mammals inherited it from an older ancestor, so it is a shared ancestral character here
A backbone is a derived character that some mammals lack, so it splits them unevenly
Backbones develop anew in each animal rather than being inherited, so they reveal nothing about ancestry
A backbone evolved separately in each mammal, so it shows convergence rather than shared ancestry

items.q: Why do researchers include an outgroup when building a cladogram from character data?
options: To show which character states are ancestral, so that derived ones can be identified
To add more taxa to the tree, since a cladogram needs at least six to be reliable
To provide the ancestor from which the members of the group descend
To measure the rate of DNA change in the group so that each node on the tree can be dated

items.q: Which kind of reproductive barrier do the data show between populations K and M?
options: Hybrid sterility: offspring form and develop, but few adults are fertile
Behavioral isolation: few K and M pairs spawn when placed together
Gametic isolation: sperm from one population rarely fertilize eggs of the other
Hybrid inviability: most fertilized K × M eggs fail to hatch

items.q: Using the biological species concept, how many species do populations K, L and M represent?
options: One
Two
Three
Unknown, since crosses do not test species

items.q: L and M rarely spawn together, but K and M spawn readily. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?
options: Where L and M meet, selection against sterile hybrids favored fish that avoid the other population
Population K lives far from M, so its fish do not yet recognize M fish as mates and avoid them
L fish are less fertile than K fish, so they spawn less with any partner, whether L or M
K and M belong to one species, while L and M belong to two different species

items.q: What is the main purpose of the K × K, L × L and M × M crosses?
options: To show what the tanks give with no barrier, so low values in mixed crosses reflect barriers
To measure how much genetic variation each population contains, so that the three can be ranked
To produce hybrid offspring whose fertility can then be compared with that of the K × M hybrids
To check whether the three populations live in the same streams, by comparing how often each spawns

items.q: Of 1,000 eggs laid in K × M crosses, how many are expected to become fertile adults, if every fish that hatches survives to adulthood? Give a whole number.
How many chromosomes are in each cell of a triploid offspring from a diploid × tetraploid cross? Give a whole number.
Why do the triploid offspring produce almost no viable seed?
options: Three copies of each chromosome cannot separate evenly in meiosis, so gametes get unbalanced sets
Triploid cells fail to complete mitosis, so the plants stop growing before they are mature enough to flower
Triploid flowers open at a different time of year from both parents, so bees rarely bring them pollen
The extra chromosome set carries recessive alleles for sterility, which are expressed in triploids

items.q: Which claim is best supported by the model?
options: The tetraploids are a new species that arose in a single generation without geographic separation
The tetraploids are the same species as the diploids, since they share a meadow and pollinators
The tetraploids became a new species through many generations of natural selection in a separate area
The tetraploids are a new species because they look different, whether or not they interbreed

items.q: Which step in the model acts as the reproductive barrier between diploids and tetraploids?
options: The triploid offspring of diploid × tetraploid crosses are sterile
The tetraploids flower at a different time from the diploids
Bees visit the tetraploids and the diploids in separate trips
Diploid × tetraploid crosses fail to form any seeds in the flowers

items.q: Which lineage shows a pattern of punctuated equilibrium, and what is the evidence?
options: Lineage Y: long stretches of little change, broken by a quick jump of 6 ribs
Lineage X: its rib number rises by about 1 rib per million years throughout
Lineage X: it ends with more ribs than lineage Y, so it changed more in total
Lineage Y: its rib number at 10 million years is higher than at the start

items.q: Calculate the mean rate of change in lineage X over the whole record, in ribs per million years. Give one decimal place.
Which hypothesis best explains the pattern in lineage Y?
options: A new form arose quickly in a small isolated population, then stabilizing selection kept it steady
Mutations happened around 4 million years, and for the rest of the record the lineage gained no new mutations
Shell ribs stopped being inherited after the jump, so no further change in rib number was possible
The same small change was added each generation, but the fossils were averaged over too many shells

items.q: A skeptic says the jump in lineage Y might only look sudden because rock layers from that time are missing. Which additional evidence would best test this?
options: Shells from a site with unbroken, closely spaced layers from 3.5 to 5 million years
More shells from each of the layers already sampled, to make each mean more precise
Shells of lineage X from the same layers, to compare its rib numbers with those of Y
Shells of living snails of lineage Y, to count the ribs on shells alive today

items.q: Put the steps of allopatric speciation in order.
options: A population is split by a geographic barrier, such as a new river channel
Gene flow between the two parts stops
Mutation, drift and different selective pressures change allele frequencies differently on each side
Differences build up that prevent interbreeding
When the barrier disappears, the two populations no longer produce fertile offspring together

items.q: Apple maggot flies mate on the fruit of the tree they grew up on. Flies whose larvae feed on apples emerge earlier in summer than flies that feed on hawthorn, matching the earlier ripening of apples, even where both trees grow side by side. Which barriers are acting between the two groups?
options: Habitat and temporal isolation (prezygotic)
Hybrid sterility and hybrid breakdown, both postzygotic
Mechanical and gametic isolation, both prezygotic
Geographic isolation, since the trees are far apart

items.q: In some land snails, the shell coils to the right in one population and to the left in another. Snails with opposite coiling cannot line up their reproductive openings and rarely mate. Which barrier is this?
options: Mechanical isolation
Behavioral isolation
Gametic isolation
Hybrid inviability

items.q: Sea urchins of two species release eggs and sperm into the same water. A sperm protein must bind a matching receptor on the egg's surface before fusion. Researchers mix eggs of species 1 with sperm of species 2. Predict the result and the barrier.
options: Few eggs are fertilized, because the sperm protein binds the foreign egg receptor poorly: gametic isolation
Many eggs are fertilized but the embryos die early, because the sperm protein is foreign: hybrid inviability
Many eggs are fertilized and the hybrids grow normally, because the gametes share the same water
Few eggs are fertilized, because the two species release gametes at different times: temporal isolation

items.q: In some crosses between two rice varieties, the first-generation hybrids are healthy and fertile, but many of their offspring are weak or sterile. Which barrier is this?
options: Hybrid breakdown
Hybrid sterility
Hybrid inviability
Gametic isolation

items.q: About 2 million years ago, a few finches reached a group of new volcanic islands with no other small land birds. Today there are over a dozen finch species there, with beaks suited to seeds, insects, cactus or buds. Which explanation best fits this adaptive radiation?
options: Open niches and isolated island populations let groups adapt to different foods and become separate species
Each finch changed its beak during its life to fit the food it ate, and passed the new beak to its chicks
The founding finches already belonged to a dozen species, which spread across the islands in different directions
With no competitors, selection stopped acting on the finches, so their beaks drifted into many forms by chance

items.q: When are biologists most likely to rely on the morphological species concept instead of the biological species concept?
options: When classifying fossils or asexual organisms, whose interbreeding is not testable
When two populations live in the same area and are known to interbreed freely
When two populations produce fertile offspring in the lab but not in the wild
When DNA sequences of the two populations are available for comparison

items.q: Select the two examples of prezygotic barriers.
options: Two frog species call with different songs, and females approach only their own species' call
Two flowering plants open their flowers in different months
A horse and a donkey produce a mule that is sterile
Two salamander species mate, but most hybrid embryos stop developing
Hybrids of two cotton species are fertile, but their offspring are weak

items.q: Two populations of a ground squirrel live on opposite rims of a deep canyon that they cannot cross. Over many generations their fur color and skull shape have become different. Which observation would most directly show that they have become separate species?
options: Squirrels from both rims mate but produce no fertile offspring
The canyon is too wide and deep for squirrels from either rim to cross
The two populations differ in the frequencies of several alleles
Each rim's squirrels eat seeds of different plants

items.q: Which statement best describes the infection data?
options: Variety H was infected far less often among rows of R than when grown alone
Variety R was infected more often when grown with variety H than when grown alone
Variety H was infected about as often in mixed fields as in fields of H alone
Variety R lost its resistance when grown in the same field as variety H

items.q: By what percent did infection of variety H fall in mixed fields compared with fields of H alone? Give a whole number.
Which explanation best accounts for variety H being infected less in the mixed fields?
options: Spores from infected H plants mostly land on R plants they cannot infect, so spread slows
Variety R plants release a chemical that kills the fungus, which protects the other plants in the field
Variety H plants grown next to variety R take up R's resistance allele through their roots
Mixed fields were planted later in the season, after the outbreak had already ended

items.q: Using the ± 2 SE values, which conclusion about yield is supported?
options: Mixed fields beat H alone but are not shown to differ from R alone
Mixed fields out-yielded both fields of H alone and fields of R alone
Fields of R alone and fields of H alone are not shown to differ from each other
The three kinds of planting are not shown to differ from one another in yield

items.q: The next year a new strain of the fungus appears that can infect variety R but not variety H. Predict which planting suffers the greatest loss.
options: Fields of R alone, because every plant is a host for the new strain
Mixed fields, because they contain two varieties the fungus can attack
Fields of H alone, because H was the variety most infected the year before
The three kinds equally, because the new strain spreads by the same kind of spores

items.q: Which statement best describes the changes from 1990-1994 to 2010-2014?
options: Heterozygosity nearly doubled while both kinds of defect became much less common
Heterozygosity fell while the population size and the share of defects both rose
The population grew, but heterozygosity and the share of defects stayed about the same
Defects became less common before any change in heterozygosity occurred

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the high rate of inherited defects in 1990-1994?
options: In a small, isolated population relatives mate, so more kittens get two copies of a harmful recessive allele
Small populations make new harmful mutations much faster, so their kittens carried many more new mutations
Low heterozygosity means kittens inherited fewer genes, so some body structures could not form
The defects were caused by the roads and farms themselves, through stress on the pregnant females

items.q: A wildlife manager claims that alleles from the released females caused the drop in defects, not better habitat. Which additional data would best test the claim?
options: Defects in same-year kittens with and without ancestry from the released females
The number of kittens born each year, compared with the number of adult females in the area
Defect rates in the larger population that the released females came from, measured in 1990-1994
The size of the area the population lived in during each period, measured from maps

items.q: A new virus that kills wild cats reaches the area. Predict how the population would have fared if the virus had arrived in 1990-1994 instead of 2010-2014.
options: Worse in 1990-1994: fewer, more similar cats made resistance alleles less likely
Better in 1990-1994: with fewer cats, the virus would have had fewer hosts and would have died out
The same in both periods, because a new virus is equally deadly to cats of any genotype
Better in 1990-1994, because inbred cats have stronger immune systems from mating with relatives

items.q: In which region do HbA HbS children survive better than HbA HbA children?
options: Where malaria is common, but not where malaria is rare
Where malaria is rare, but not where malaria is common
In both regions, by about the same amount
In neither region; HbA HbA survives best in both

items.q: HbS HbS children rarely survive to adulthood, yet the HbS allele stays common where malaria is common. Which explanation fits the graph?
options: Carriers, who hold most HbS alleles, survive better than either homozygote, so both alleles stay
New HbS mutations arise each generation fast enough to replace the alleles lost in HbS HbS children
Malaria causes the HbA allele to change into the HbS allele in people who are infected
The HbS allele is dominant, so it spreads whether or not it helps the people who carry it

items.q: In a population where malaria is common, the frequency of the HbS allele is 0.10. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg proportions among newborns, what percent of newborns are HbA HbS carriers? Give a whole number.
Malaria is wiped out in the first region and does not return for many generations. No modern medical care is available. Predict the change in each quantity over those generations.

variables.name: Rate at which new HbS mutations arise

items.q: Nearly every export banana is a Cavendish, grown from cuttings of a few original plants. A fungal disease that kills Cavendish plants has spread to many countries. Why is the crop so vulnerable?
options: The plants are clones, so a strain that can infect one plant can infect nearly all of them
Bananas grown from cuttings mutate faster than bananas grown from seed, so they lose resistance quickly
Fungi infect plants grown from cuttings more easily than plants of any kind grown from seed
The Cavendish was bred for flavor, and flavor genes make plants more attractive to fungi

items.q: In the 1840s, most potatoes grown in Ireland belonged to a single variety, propagated from pieces of tubers. When a water mold that rots potatoes arrived, most of the crop was destroyed for several years. Which evidence would best support the claim that low genetic variation, rather than bad weather alone, caused the scale of the loss?
options: In the same years, regions growing several varieties lost a much smaller share of their crops
The summers of those years were cooler and wetter than average, which favors the spread of the water mold
Potatoes from the single variety gave high yields in the years before the water mold arrived
The water mold had been reported in the Americas a few years before it reached Ireland

items.q: About 1% of people of northern European ancestry carry two copies of an allele, CCR5-Δ32, that removes a receptor most HIV strains use to enter cells, and they resist infection by those strains. What does this show about variation in populations?
options: Variation already present can include alleles that let some people survive a new disease
HIV caused the CCR5-Δ32 allele to arise in people who were exposed to the virus
A population needs no variation, because one resistant person can protect everyone else
Variation matters for crops but not for human populations, which rely on medicine

items.q: Select the two populations most vulnerable to being wiped out by a new disease.
options: A field of potato plants grown from tubers of one plant
A herd of 40 cattle descended from 4 founders, closely inbred for generations
A large wild population of field mice that breeds with nearby populations
A wild grass population of 100,000 plants pollinated by wind across a wide area
A sexually reproducing population of 50,000 frogs in a large wetland

items.q: A small fish of the Atlantic coast carries two common alleles of a gene for the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase. One allele's enzyme works faster in cold water; it is most frequent in the north and rare in the south. How does this variation help the species?
options: Each allele's enzyme works best at a different temperature, so each region's fish suit local water
Fish in the north switch to the cold-water allele when the water cools in winter
The cold-water allele is dominant, so it spreads into the southern populations over time
Having two alleles lets each fish make twice as much enzyme as a fish with one allele

items.q: Seed banks store seeds of old crop varieties and wild relatives of crops, even ones with low yields. Which reason best justifies this?
options: They keep alleles missing from today's uniform crops, which breeders may need for future threats
Old varieties grow faster than modern ones, so they can replace modern crops when yields fall
Seeds in storage mutate into new varieties, giving breeders a supply of new alleles
Storing many varieties lets farmers plant one variety everywhere, which reduces crop losses

items.q: Which population is most likely to include some individuals able to survive a sudden environmental change?
options: A large population with high variation
A small population with low genetic variation
A population of genetically identical clones
A population descended from two founders

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: With sparks, both rose fast at first and then slowly, glycine staying higher
With sparks, alanine built up faster than glycine and passed it after about 3 days
Amino acids appeared in both kinds of flask, but more slowly without sparks
With sparks, both amino acids rose at a steady rate for the full 7 days

items.q: Calculate the mean rate at which glycine formed in the sparked flasks during the first 2 days, in µmol per day. Give one decimal place.
What do the no-spark control flasks allow the students to conclude?
options: The sparks' energy made the amino acids; contamination or the gases alone did not
Amino acids break down when no energy is supplied, so they need to be made continuously
The gases in the flasks were the same as those in the air of Earth when it first formed
Living cells are needed to turn the amino acids into proteins inside the flasks

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the slowing of amino acid formation after day 4?
options: The sealed flasks' starting gases were being used up, so less product formed daily
The amino acids joined into living cells, which then used up the remaining gases
The electrodes stopped making sparks after day 4, so no more energy entered the flasks
Glycine was converted into alanine, which kept the total amount of amino acid the same

items.q: Many geologists now think the early atmosphere was mostly carbon dioxide and nitrogen, with little methane or ammonia. Which next experiment would best test whether amino acids could still have formed?
options: Repeat it with carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water vapor instead of the original gases
Repeat the experiment with the same gases, but run the sparks for 30 days instead of 7
Repeat the experiment with the same gases, but add amino acids at the start to see if they last
Repeat the experiment with the same gases in open flasks, so that air can enter as needed

items.q: Which statement best describes the effect of clay?
options: Clay made vesicles form about 85 times faster, whether or not RNA was present
Clay made vesicles form about 85 times slower, because it took up the fatty acid
Clay sped up vesicle formation just when RNA was stuck to it
Clay had no effect on vesicle formation but raised the share holding RNA

items.q: How many times more vesicles contained RNA when the RNA was stuck to clay than when free RNA was added? Give a whole number.
Which explanation best accounts for far more vesicles containing RNA when the RNA was stuck to clay?
options: Vesicles formed on clay surfaces, so they wrapped around the RNA stuck there
Clay broke RNA into single nucleotides, which pass through vesicle membranes more easily
RNA on clay acted as an enzyme that built the vesicle membranes out of fatty acids
Clay removed the fatty acids from the water, so the RNA filled the space left behind

items.q: The same kind of clay also helps join activated nucleotides into RNA chains. Why does this make clay interesting to scientists studying the origin of life?
options: One surface could help both build RNA and enclose it, linking two steps toward a protocell
It shows that clay was the first living thing, because it can copy itself and form membranes
It proves that life began in clay-rich soils rather than in the oceans or at hydrothermal vents on the sea floor
It shows that membranes formed before any monomers, so RNA was not needed for the first cells

items.q: According to the table, which molecule can both store information and catalyze reactions in cells?
options: RNA
DNA
Protein
DNA and protein together

items.q: In every ribosome, the site that joins amino acids into a chain is made of rRNA, not protein. How does this support the RNA world hypothesis?
options: Protein synthesis relies on an RNA catalyst, as expected if RNA catalysts came first
It shows that rRNA stores the genetic information for each of the proteins the cell makes
It shows that proteins fold correctly just when rRNA holds them in shape
It shows that the ribosome evolved after DNA, so DNA came before RNA

items.q: If RNA came first, why would DNA later have replaced it as the main store of genetic information?
options: DNA lacks the 2′ –OH that helps break RNA, so long sequences last and copy reliably
DNA can catalyze more kinds of reactions than RNA, so it could also take over the jobs of enzymes
DNA has 20 different building blocks, so it can store more information per unit than RNA
DNA is made without any template, so cells with DNA no longer needed to copy their genes

items.q: In the lab, researchers have made a ribozyme that copies other RNA strands, with some errors. Predict what would happen in a population of such ribozymes copying one another over many rounds, with limited nucleotides.
options: Better-copying variants would become more common: natural selection on molecules
Each copy would match the first ribozyme exactly, because base pairing prevents change
The ribozymes would turn into DNA, because DNA is the more stable molecule
The ribozymes would stop copying, because copying with errors destroys the molecules

items.q: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago, and the oldest widely accepted fossils are about 3.5 billion years old. For what percent of Earth's history is there fossil evidence of life? Give a whole number.

Stromatolites are rock mounds with fine layers. Today they form in a few warm, salty bays where mats of cyanobacteria trap sediment and grow upward through it. Rocks about 3.5 billion years old contain similar layered mounds. What do the ancient mounds best support?
options: Mats of microbes existed about 3.5 billion years ago and built layered mounds as modern mats do
Cyanobacteria filled the oceans 3.5 billion years ago and made the air rich in oxygen at that time
Life arose in warm, salty bays 3.5 billion years ago, where the mounds formed
Layers in any old rock prove that living things were present when it formed

items.q: Select the two conditions that scientists think were true of early Earth when life began.
options: Little or no free oxygen in the atmosphere
Frequent volcanic activity and impacts from space
An ozone layer blocking most ultraviolet light
Forests of land plants releasing oxygen
Oceans already full of organic molecules made by cells

items.q: In water, amino acids and nucleotides tend not to join into long chains. Why might mineral surfaces such as clay, or pools that dry and refill, have helped polymers form?
options: They concentrate monomers and remove water, favoring dehydration synthesis
They add water to the monomers, favoring the hydrolysis reactions that build chains
They provide oxygen, which the joining reactions use as an energy source
They hold the monomers far apart so that they do not react with the wrong partner

items.q: Some scientists propose that life began at hydrothermal vents on the sea floor. Which feature of vents best supports this hypothesis?
options: Hot, mineral-rich water meeting cold seawater gives chemical energy and catalytic surfaces
Vents receive strong sunlight, which drives photosynthesis in the earliest cells
Vents are rich in free oxygen, which early cells used for respiration
Vents are cold and stable, which keeps fragile RNA from ever breaking down

items.q: Put these proposed steps toward the first cells in order.
options: Simple inorganic molecules react, using energy from lightning, UV light or vents
Monomers such as amino acids and nucleotides accumulate
Monomers join into polymers such as RNA on mineral surfaces
Membranes of fatty acids enclose self-copying RNA, forming protocells
DNA takes over information storage and proteins take over most catalysis

items.q: If simple molecules could form life on early Earth, why do new life forms not arise from nonliving chemicals today?
options: Oxygen breaks down organic molecules today, and microbes would eat any that formed
The laws of chemistry have changed since early Earth, so the same reactions no longer happen
Lightning and volcanoes no longer occur, so there is no energy to build organic molecules
Living things today release chemicals that turn simple molecules into carbon dioxide on contact
